papers.title: Contact-phagy remodels ER-mitochondria contact sites
papers.abstract: Membrane contact sites between the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and other organelles coordinate cellular organization, metabolism and stress responses, yet how these interfaces are selectively remodeled and removed remains poorly understood. Here we identify a selective autophagy pathway that targets defined ER-mitochondria contact-site (ERMCS) subdomains for turnover, a process we term Contact-phagy. The ER-resident chaperone SIGMAR1 forms a functional complex with the ER-phagy receptor CCPG1, and SIGMAR1-CCPG1 nanoclusters define ERMCS-associated sites of autophagy initiation. Contact-phagy is selectively engaged by metabolic and mitochondrial stress and promotes turnover of defined contact-site components without broadly affecting general ER-phagy, mitophagy or bulk autophagy. At these sites, SIGMAR1-CCPG1 function is coupled to mitochondrial fission: MFF promotes DRP1 recruitment to ERMCS, whereas loss of CCPG1 or SIGMAR1 causes abnormal persistence and clustering of DRP1 and MFF, accompanied by altered mitochondrial remodeling. Loss of CCPG1 further disrupts ER-mitochondria organization and mitochondrial function in pancreatic tissue, while pancreatic cancer cells depend on CCPG1 and SIGMAR1 for organelle integrity and bioenergetic capacity. Together, our findings establish Contact-phagy as a selective pathway for the turnover of defined organelle contact site subdomains and suggest a broader principle by which interorganelle interfaces are maintained.

papers.title: The infectious unit of influenza A virus is a population of particles, not a single virion, as shown by absolute particle quantification
papers.abstract: Influenza A virus (IAV) populations are characterized by a high prevalence of non-infectious virions, with particle-to-plaque forming unit (PFU) ratios typically ranging from 10 to 1,000. While "multiplicity reactivation" -the process by which incomplete viral genomes (IVGs) establish productive infection through co-infection- has long been hypothesized, its quantitative nature has remained elusive. In this study, we utilized a digital influenza assay to achieve absolute quantification of IAV particles, allowing us to define the particle-based multiplicity of infection (pMOI) for precise evaluation. We combined this approach with a single-cell infection assay using microcompartmentalized containers and machine learning-based automated cell classification to accurately assess infection outcomes across a wide range of pMOIs. Our analysis of the A/Puerto Rico/8/1934 (H1N1) revealed a count-to-plaque forming unit (PFU) ratio of approximately 400, meaning only a tiny fraction of particles possesses infectivity. Remarkably, the infection rate in single-cell infection experiments followed a sigmoidal curve and reached saturation at a pMOI of only 5 to 10. This demonstrates that under high-pMOI conditions, productive infection is predominantly driven by genome complementation among incomplete particles rather than solely by fully infectious virions. On the other hand, mathematical model analysis based on these findings suggested that the functionality of each of the eight genomic segments within a virus particle follows a stochastic process, resulting in a probability distribution for the number of functional segments per particle. This mechanism proved exceptionally robust across multiple strains despite a 20-fold variation in CTPR values. Ultimately, these findings indicate that incomplete particles are not merely biological noise but active contributors to the infection process, significantly enhancing the infectivity and evolutionary flexibility of IAV. This study will provide a more refined understanding of influenza transmission dynamics and risk assessment, particularly in environments where multiple virus particles are present within a single respiratory droplet.

papers.title: A conserved tyrosine in the S1/S2 loop shapes SARS-CoV-2 spike processing and host protease usage.
papers.abstract: Both spike processing efficiency and host protease usage play critical roles in SARS-CoV-2 infection, pathogenesis, and transmission. The SARS-CoV-2 spike contains two motifs, a furin cleavage site (FCS) and an extended S1/S2 loop, which improve both cleavage efficiency and host protease usage. Disruption of these motifs significantly attenuates SARS-CoV-2 infection and pathogenesis. Importantly, modifications and changes within the S1/S2 loop can also shape infection and disease outcomes following infection. In this study, we examined mass spectrometry data generated from purified virions from wild-type (WT) or mutant SARS-CoV-2 infection. We identified phosphorylation occurring at highly conserved residue Y674 and used reverse genetics to generate a mutant that ablates phosphorylation capacity in the S1/ S2 loop (Y674F). Our results show that the Y674F mutant replicated equivalently to wild-type SARS-CoV-2 in Vero cells but had attenuated replication in a human respiratory cell line. Golden Syrian hamsters infected with the Y674F mutant had equivalent weight loss, lung viral titer, and similar immune pathology to WT SARS-CoV-2. However, the mutant had reduced viral load in the nasal wash and reduced antigen staining in the large airways in the lung. Notably, loss of Y674 ablated spike processing to the S1/S2 cleavage product on virions. In addition, Y674F mutant had a diminished capacity to utilize host protease TMPRSS2 for entry. Together, these data indicates that post-translational modification of Y674 impacts SARS-CoV-2 infection of the airway by disrupting both spike processing and host protease function. These results add to data demonstrating the importance of spike S1/S2 loop modifications to SARS-CoV-2 infection, pathogenesis, and transmission.

papers.title: mRNA-LNP vaccination induces microenvironment remodeling and generation of tissue-resident memory T cells in glioblastoma
papers.abstract: Glioblastoma remains highly refractory to immunotherapy, in part because of a profoundly immunosuppressive tumour microenvironment that limits effective T-cell responses. Although mRNA vaccines can induce anti-tumour immunity, how they reshape the glioblastoma immune ecosystem to support durable tumour control is not well understood. Here we use an immunocompetent EGFRvIII-driven syngeneic glioblastoma model and antigen-specific mRNA lipid nanoparticle (mRNA-LNP) vaccination to define the cellular and spatial mechanisms underlying therapeutic response. In our model, vaccination induced durable EGFRvIII-specific humoral and cellular immunity, resulting in complete tumour eradication and long-term protection against intracranial rechallenge. Integrative analyses incorporating flow cytometry, tumour interstitial fluid profiling, multiplex immunostaining, spatial transcriptomics and ligand-receptor modelling demonstrated extensive remodelling of the tumour microenvironment following vaccination. Early tumour control was associated with expansion of pro-inflammatory and antigen-presenting myeloid populations, increased cytotoxic CD8 T-cell infiltration and activation, enhanced interferon-responsive signalling, and the formation of immune-supportive spatial niches enriched for antigen presentation and chemokine-mediated cellular communication. Vaccination promoted inflammatory chemokine relay networks centred on the CXCL16-CXCR6 axis, a pathway linked to tissue residency programming in the central nervous system. Functional depletion studies identified CD4 and CD8 T cells as essential mediators of therapeutic efficacy, while durable protection was maintained by tumour-specific brain-resident memory CD8 T cells that persisted despite peripheral lymphocyte depletion. Together, these findings identify T-cell-driven microenvironmental remodelling as a critical mechanism linking mRNA vaccination to the establishment of long-term brain-resident anti-tumour immunity in glioblastoma.

papers.title: Phage peptide promotes bacterial cell death via inner and outer membrane targets
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Cationic antimicrobial peptides (CAMPs) play a major role in mammalian innate immunity by preferentially targeting bacterial membranes through charge-dependent interactions. While CAMPs are extensively studied in eukaryotic systems, less is known about phage-encoded CAMPs and their role in bacterial lysis. Here, we characterize gp28, a 56-aa cationic peptide encoded by the T7-like coliphage phiKT to define its mechanism of membrane disruption and bacteriostatic activity. Biochemical fractionation reveals that gp28 is asymmetrically distributed across bacterial membranes. Supporting its direct role in causing cell death, gp28 induces permeability changes at the inner membrane. Using synthetic gp28 peptide, we also show that gp28 activity is blocked by lipopolysaccharide and divalent cation competition. This led us to discover that gp28 is also active against Gram-positive bacteria in a surface charge-dependent manner. Finally, we demonstrate gp28 has broad bacteriostatic activity against multiple Gram-negative species, including clinical Uropathogenic E. coli (UPEC) isolates. Together, our results support a model in which gp28 exploits charge-based interactions with bacterial surface molecules to gain access to membranes, then destabilizes the envelope to promote host cell death. These findings expand our understanding of phage lysis strategies and highlight phage-derived peptides as potential scaffolds for antimicrobial development. SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT Cationic antimicrobial peptides produced by eukaryotes target and disrupt bacterial membranes. These peptides are integral members of the innate immune system and potential antibacterials. Due to their cellular origin, the genetics to understand their mechanisms of action are cumbersome. Here, we demonstrate functional similarity between a bacteriophage peptide called gp28 and cationic antimicrobial peptides. Gp28 partitions between both membranes of Gram-negative bacteria and reduces their integrity. We show that gp28 employs charge-based interactions to associate with and disrupt membranes, suggesting that gp28 targets charged polymers on the membrane surface. Additionally, gp28 inhibits the growth of Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, and renders them more susceptible to antibiotics. Our studies provide a foundation for future genetics and development of phage peptide-based antimicrobials.

papers.title: Multi-specific nanobody-Fc fusions against TcdB protect in vivo from diverse Clostridioides difficile strains
papers.abstract: Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) is an urgent antibiotic-associated threat and the leading cause of nosocomial diarrhea in the United States, with a high rate of recurrence. Antibiotics are the standard of care for treating CDI but can prolong microbial dysbiosis in the gut. The only FDA-approved monoclonal antibody (mAb) for the prevention of recurrent CDI, Zinplava (bezlotoxumab), was discontinued in January 2025. The target of bezlotoxumab is the dominant virulence factor of C. difficile, the exotoxin B (TcdB). However, TcdB sequences vary across strains and encompass twelve distinct subtypes. Consequently, sequence variation between subtypes presents a challenge for the identification of pan-neutralizing mAb therapeutics. Here, we describe the generation of three bi-specific and one tri-specific nanobody-Fc fusions targeting TcdB. Each fusion neutralizes TcdB in vitro across clinically relevant subtypes with greater potency than bezlotoxumab. In a mouse model of CDI, using three diverse C. difficile strains, several of the fusion proteins improve infection outcomes over bezlotoxumab when administered prophylactically. We also highlight one fusion that improves survival in a therapeutic mouse model of CDI. These data demonstrate multi-specific nanobody-Fc fusions as a strategy to improve potency and mitigate the impact of sequence variation within the toxin. Our fusions outperform the standards established by bezlotoxumab and represent strong candidates for translation.

papers.title: Darwinian and Wallacean evolution both explain sexual dichromatism in avian iridescence.
papers.abstract: One of the longest-standing arguments in evolutionary biology is that between Darwin and Wallace on the evolution of sexual dichromatism, and which sex changed colour over time. While Darwin argued that males became more colourful over time, Wallace argued that females became less colourful, and numerous studies have lent support to each hypothesis over time. Iridescent colouration provides a particularly interesting system for studying sexual dichromatism because its conspicuousness is often associated with sexual selection and it has evolved multiple times. Here, using a dataset on iridescent colouration of 25,432 patches from 3,151 bird species, we provide one of the most comprehensive tests to date of the evolutionary origins of sexual dichromatism. We show that both hypotheses explain the evolution of iridescent sexual dichromatism in birds, but that Darwin's hypothesis is more strongly supported with males contributing stronger to evolutionary changes in dichromatism. Furthermore, our analyses support Darwin's prediction that sexual selection is associated to the evolution of dichromatism, but also Wallace's prediction that safer nests facilitate more colourful females (and males), and mostly in patches exposed during incubation.

papers.title: Multivalent BBSome-IFT proximities support IFT-A-IFT-B coordination in vivo
papers.abstract: Intraflagellar transport (IFT) depends on coordinated movement of IFT-A and IFT-B, yet how these assemblies remain coupled within dynamic ciliary trains is unclear. Here, we combine endogenous fluorescent knock-in tagging, quantitative in vivo FLIM-FRET, structural modeling, and targeted mutagenesis to define IFT organization in C. elegans and mammalian cells. FLIM-FRET mapping identifies proximity networks within IFT-B and places IFT144 near IFT172 and IFT88 in intact cilia. Loss of BBSome function is associated with weaker IFT-A-IFT-B proximity signals and divergent subcomplex transport dynamics, consistent with a contribution of the BBSome to IFT coordination in vivo. Split-GFP complementation places BBSome components near IFT-A and IFT-B, while structural modeling nominates complementary charged surfaces on the IFT46-IFT52 dimer and BBS7/BBS9. Charge-reversal mutations targeting these surfaces impair BBSome recruitment and functional rescue. Together, these findings support a model in which multivalent BBSome-IFT proximities contribute to IFT-A-IFT-B coordination during ciliary transport.

papers.title: bofasa enables high-quality orthology inference across diverse multi-species bacterial genome sets
papers.abstract: Bacterial species can be separated by billions of years of evolution. However, studies of such ancient relationships often rely on methods developed for eukaryotes, which are less diverse. Such methods can regard instances of horizontal gene transfer as contamination, rely heavily on a species phylogeny when partitioning paralogs, and fail to account for the multi-domain architectures of some genes. Here, we introduce, showcase, and benchmark bofasa, a software for high-quality and automated inference of ortholog groups across distantly related bacterial species. bofasa employs a recursive algorithm to split coarse homolog groups into paralogous subsets and first establishes domain-level ortholog groups prior to assessing evolutionary relationships between entire proteins. In comparison to other methods commonly used for multi-species bacterial comparative genomics, bofasa is substantially more conservative in predicting orthology yet can often recover the largest single-copy core genome. Beyond orthology inference, the software also features several additional utility functionalities, including assessment of which ortholog groups are commonly found on mobile genetic elements or possess variable genomic contexts.

papers.title: Exploring taxonomic diversity in the genus Suberites Nardo, 1833: Insights from microbial, phylogenetic, and morphological analyses
papers.abstract: Marine sponges (phylum Porifera) are a highly diverse and polymorphic group of marine invertebrates whose taxonomic delimitation is often challenging due to high intraspecific variability and the scarcity of diagnostic morphological characters. Their close association with microbial symbionts also makes them an important source of secondary metabolites, some of which may contribute to sponge colouration. Here, we use morphological characters, molecular phylogenetic markers, and 16S metabarcoding of the symbiont community to understand speciation in a common Mediterranean sponge lineage. We collected 43 specimens of the genus Suberites from the Mediterranean Sea and the North and South Atlantic Oceans, between 55-150 m depths, and sequenced two barcoding genes, cytochrome c oxidase I and 28S rDNA, as well as studied their spicular complements. We identified five closely-related species: S. domuncula, S. ficus/pagurorum, S. dandelenae, S. ambulodomus, and a new species of Suberites from the Balearic Islands, Suberites sp. nov. The latter represents a potential new pseudo-cryptic species closely related to S. domuncula, because of their strong morphological and molecular affinities. The potential new Mediterranean species exhibits six colour morphotypes (yellow, gray, orange, brown, red, and blue), and the microbiome analyses of the symbiotic communities revealed significant differences in bacterial community composition among colour morphotypes, specially of bacteria that produce different pigments which potentially give the sponge is colouration. These results provide valuable insights into species boundaries and evolutionary relationships within the genus Suberites and support a role for the microbiome in sponge colouration.

papers.title: Loss of the mitochondrial redox gene GLRX2 underlies somersaulting behavior in Darwin's pigeons
papers.abstract: Darwin described the somersaulting behavior of pigeons as "one of the most remarkable inherited habits ever recorded", yet its molecular basis remained unknown. We show that somersaulting pigeon brains exhibit mitochondrial redox dysfunction and identify an 11-bp frameshifting deletion in GLRX2, a mitochondrial redox enzyme, that abolishes protein function and is highly-enriched in two independently selected breeds. GLRX2 deficiency in mice and zebrafish recapitulates mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress and impaired motor coordination seen in pigeons. Single-nucleus transcriptomics identifies cerebellar Golgi and Purkinje cells as selectively vulnerable, with disrupted inhibitory signaling and synaptic remodeling. These findings demonstrate how relaxation of purifying selection during domestication can expose a deleterious mitochondrial variant to artificial selection, allowing gene loss to serve as a substrate for behavioral evolution.

papers.title: The extracellular morphology and behaviour of the last common ancestor of animals and choanoflagellates
papers.abstract: Choanoflagellates, the closest known living relatives of animals, provide a powerful comparative system for investigating the evolution of extracellular morphology and cell behaviour on the animal stem lineage. Although all choanoflagellates share a conserved cellular architecture including a flagellum and collar of microvilli, they display a wide diversity of extracellular structures and behaviours throughout the life cycle. Their extracellular features, historically used for species identification, have long been suspected to reflect a mixture of evolutionary inheritance and ecological plasticity. Yet, the majority of choanoflagellate diversity remains undescribed, and the extent to which their extracellular traits map onto their phylogeny has remained unclear, impeding comparative reconstructions of the evolutionary history of extracellular structures with the earliest animals. Here, we integrate super-resolution fluorescence imaging, electron microscopy and transcriptomic analysis to characterize the extracellular structures and behaviours across both currently described lineages of choanoflagellates (Craspedida and Acanthoecida), by studying pairs of closely related species in conjunction with novel isolates representing previously unexplored clades. Our results reveal strong conservation of extracellular morphology between close relatives, whereas deeper evolutionary distances uncover unexpected innovations, such as sheath-like layers, bipartite thecae, crawling stages and atypical inverted division patterns. Furthermore, the inclusion of early-branching taxa sister to the loricates supports the hypothesis that the silicified extracellular lorica is a derived trait rather than an ancestral feature. Together, our findings suggest that the last choanoflagellate common ancestor possessed an organic non-silicified extracellular covering composed of one or more layers and that it was capable of both swimming and crawling behaviours, refining the cellular context from which animals evolved.

papers.title: An interplay of multilayered regulatory mechanisms underlies the RNA solubility phase transition during vertebrate oocyte-to-embryo transition
papers.abstract: Dynamic RNA-protein interactions influence RNA transport, storage, stability, and activity and are fundamental to a broad range of biological processes. During the oocyte-to-embryo transition (OET), fully differentiated gametes fuse and regain totipotency. Throughout the OET, the transcription remains silent. Spatiotemporal regulation of gene expression relies on the dynamic interactions between maternal transcripts and various protein complexes. Despite its fundamental importance, RNA-protein interaction dynamics at the global level during the OET remain poorly understood. Here, we leverage fractionation RNA-seq to profile RNA insolubility, a proxy for the interaction between RNAs and protein complexes, during zebrafish OET. We identify transcripts that transition between the soluble (relatively protein-free) and insoluble (heavily protein-associated) states and demonstrate that these phase transitions are driven by ribosome-dependent and ribosome-independent mechanisms. We demonstrate that the capacity of maternal RNAs to engage with protein complexes changes dynamically during the OET through remodeling of cis-regulatory features. We developed a machine-learning framework and uncovered multiple cis- and trans-regulatory features that may contribute to RNA insolubility. To validate these predictions, we examined poly(A) tail length and m6A dynamics. We found that poly(A) tail length is associated with both ribosome-dependent and ribosome-independent RNA phase transitions. In parallel, fractionation m6A-pulldown RNA-seq revealed highly dynamic changes in the m6A landscape during the OET. A correlation between m6A modifications and RNA insolubility is gradually established during the OET. Together, our findings uncover a multilayered regulatory mechanism governing RNA phase transitions during the OET, providing fundamental insights into post-transcriptional regulation of gene expression during development.

papers.title: Global mapping of VEGF-A driven changes in the RNA bound phospho-proteome reveals a molecular switch to coordinate angiogenesis in endothelial cells
papers.abstract: RNA binding proteins (RBPs) serve as upstream master regulators of cellular fate transitions at the post-transcriptional level. RBP-RNA interactions are dynamically regulated by post-translational modifications to coordinate cellular responses. We hypothesised that changes in RBP phosphorylation will play a key role in coordinating angiogenesis, the formation of new blood vessels, in endothelial cells (ECs). Therefore, we used phospho-proteomic analysis of the mRNA bound proteome to identify global phosphorylation changes in mouse cardiac ECs during acute and prolonged VEGF-A stimulation. Of the differentially phosphorylated RBPs, we found that the phosphorylation of serine 199 within mRNA bound Phf6 (PHD finger protein 6) was consistently increased following VEGF-A stimulation. Phf6 phosphorylation at this specific site was sufficient and required to induce a pro-angiogenic phenotype, facilitating a change in Phf6 conformation promoting interaction with distinct RNAs. We show here that Phf6 phosphorylation at serine 199, downstream of VEGF-A, acts as a molecular switch to differentially coordinate a decrease of anti-angiogenic RNAs (i.e. extracellular matrix genes) and an increase in pro-angiogenesis related RNAs, in part by differentially regulating their stability, to promote angiogenesis.

papers.title: Uncoupling Osteoclast Fusion and Resorptive Activity Through Differential Talin1-Rap1 Signalling Pathways
papers.abstract: Bone remodelling is essential for skeletal growth and repair and depends on a balance between osteoblast-driven bone formation and osteoclast-mediated bone resorption. Integrin activation, regulated by Rap1 and Talin1, is critical for osteoclast function by coordinated adhesion and actin cytoskeleton organization. In this study, we investigated Rap1 effectors controlling Talin1 in osteoclasts. RIAM and Lamellipodin (Lpd) are expressed and localise to actin-rich structures, including tunneling nanotubes (TNTs) and podosomes, supporting roles in cytoskeletal organisation and intercellular connectivity. Functional analyses revealed distinct, stage-specific functions. Lpd deficiency impaired early osteoclastogenesis by reducing TNT formation, disrupting precursor fusion, decreasing multinucleation, and lowering bone resorption. In contrast, RIAM deficiency has minimal impact on fusion but significantly reduced resorption activity in mature osteoclasts, indicating a role at later stages. Disruption of the direct Rap1-Talin1 interaction caused broader defects affecting both early and late stages, including reduced TNT formation, delayed fusion, altered multinucleation, and impaired bone degradation. In vivo, only disruption of this direct interaction increased bone mass and reduced osteoclast number and/or activity, whereas RIAM or Lpd deletion had no significantly impact. These results demonstrate that RIAM and Lpd perform distinct but complementary functions and identify the direct Rap1-Talin1 interaction as a central mechanism controlling osteoclast fusion and bone resorption.

papers.title: RAMP-Seq: a single-tube nanopore workflow for co-amplifying full-length 16S rRNA and antimicrobial resistance genes for integrated taxonomic and resistance profiling
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance needs workflows that both identify bacteria and detect resistance genes from a single sample, but current targeted nanopore assays typically split these steps into separate reactions or library preparations. We introduce RAMP-Seq (Rapid AMR Profiling by Sequencing), a workflow that simultaneously amplifies the full-length 16S rRNA gene (~1,500 bp) together with eight resistance determinants (~600 - 700 bp) in a single multiplex PCR and then sequences the resulting mixed-length amplicon pool as a single nanopore library. The eight-primer pair set targets dominant alleles of {beta}-lactamase, carbapenemase, quinolone-resistance and silver-resistance families. Read-length distributions confirmed that both size classes were co-amplified evenly using a single, non-equimolar primer pool. From extracted DNA to the first taxonomically classified reads took 8.2 {+/-} 0.6 h. Full-length 16S sequencing of an eight-member mock community identified all anticipated taxa, and the observed abundances closely followed the expected log-scaled composition (Pearson's r = 0.879). The full nineplex amplicon assay was subsequently tested on three distinct matrices: pooled clinical isolates, spiked human blood, and environmental water samples. Using an equal-mass pool of genomic DNA from eleven multidrug-resistant clinical and repository isolates, the full assay produced genus-level and resistance-gene profiles that were consistent across biological replicates (r = 0.998 and r = 0.824), and it specifically identified all seven panel targets present, confirmed by Illumina whole-genome sequencing. After carbonate-based host DNA depletion, Klebsiella pneumoniae was recovered from spiked human blood at every titration down to 102 CFU/mL, as were all five panel targets carried by that strain. Across five water-sampling sites from a sewage treatment plant (STP) to a connected lake system, microbial communities and resistance-gene profiles were site-specific: influent and effluent communities overlapped little, while the lake inlet and outlet were similar. Target resistance genes were most numerous and abundant in STP influent, fewer in effluent, and rare or absent in lake and well samples. Because bacterial identification relies on amplification of the conserved, near-universal 16S rRNA gene, rather than on species-specific primer sets, RAMP-Seq can detect and taxonomically classify bacteria in a design-agnostic manner. The same single-tube chemistry therefore serves sample types as different as clinical specimens and environmental water and is extendable to longer ribosomal targets and further resistance-gene families.

papers.title: Development of African Swine Fever Virus Pseudotype Systems for Ba71v and Georgia 2007 strains
papers.abstract: African swine fever virus (ASFV) is a large, complex DNA virus that causes a severe haemorrhagic disease in domestic swine and Eurasian wild boar. Due to its high pathogenicity, research involving ASFV is restricted to high-containment laboratories, which significantly limits investigations into its biology, host interactions and the development of effective control measures. To overcome these limitations, this study utilised pseudotyped virus (PV) technology to identify ASFV proteins involved in cell entry. Candidate proteins were identified through bioinformatic analysis and a review of the published literature, incorporated into PVs, and subsequently assessed for their ability to facilitate cellular entry. This approach identified a combination of three ASFV proteins that, when combined, resulted in the most efficient cell entry. This work represents the successful generation of the first functional ASF pseudotype system for both Ba71v and Georgia 2007 strains, enabling the safe study of ASFV entry mechanisms under containment level 2.

papers.title: A polarized genome is required for fitness of the obligate intracellular, tick-borne pathogen Rickettsia parkeri
papers.abstract: Alphaproteobacteria of the order Rickettsiales include biomedically important, yet understudied arthropod-borne human pathogens. These pathogens lack obvious morphological asymmetry, but encode homologs of key mediators of polar processes in the model Alphaproteobacterium Caulobacter crescentus. These include the polar organizing protein PopZ, the chromosome segregation proteins ParA and ParB, and the spatial regulator of cell division MipZ. Motivated by this observation, we used the tick-borne human pathogen Rickettsia parkeri to ask if the chromosome is polarized and coordinated with cell division in this group. Consistent with that hypothesis, we found that transposon insertion mutants in parA, parB, mipZ, or popZ resulted in cell division defects. Fluorescence imaging revealed cell cycle-dependent unipolar-to-bipolar localization dynamics of ParB and MipZ, and pole-to-midcell dynamics of the division protein ZapA. This patterning parallels the model of chromosome segregation and cell division site selection established in Caulobacter. Unlike its unipolar-to-bipolar dynamics in Caulobacter, however, PopZ remained at a single cell pole throughout the cell cycle in R. parkeri. PopZ maintained its direct interaction with ParA and ParB. Interestingly, disruption of parA or parB, but not popZ or mipZ, caused a small plaque phenotype, suggesting a defect in growth or spread in a monolayer of host cells in the absence of proper chromosome segregation. We propose that genome polarization in R. parkeri and other rickettsiae is critical both for fundamental cellular processes and for interactions with host cells that promote fitness in their infectious niche.

papers.title: EveD, a vesicle-associated rhizobial candidate effector shaping nodulation competitiveness and host genotype responses
papers.abstract: Bacterial extracellular vesicles (EVs) are an ancestral secretion route that delivers cargoes to host cells. Although rhizobial EVs transport Nod factors and other bacterial components, their role in protein delivery during symbiosis remains unexplored. Here we characterise EveD, a large soluble repeat-containing protein of Sinorhizobium fredii HH103. Its export is independent of the type III secretion system, and EveD is recovered only in EV-containing fractions. eveD expression is not induced by genistein or soybean seed exudates and does not follow the canonical NodD1-TtsI pathway, but partially depends on the symbiotic regulator SyrM. When expressed in plant cells, EveD localises mainly to the cytoplasm, associates with endoplasmic reticulum-like structures and occasionally occurs in the nucleus. The eveD mutant shows increased nodule occupancy relative to the wild type in Glycine max cv. Williams 82. EveD modulates early responses in wild Glycine soja accessions in a genotype-dependent manner, constraining pseudonodule organogenesis in JL2 while promoting it in CH2. These findings identify EveD as an EV-associated rhizobial protein contributing to bacterial competitiveness and genotype-dependent symbiotic responses, and highlight EVs as an additional route for protein export during legume symbiosis.

papers.title: Adaptive tracking contributes to the invasion success of a global pest insect
papers.abstract: Invasive species are a threat to biodiversity, natural resources, and the economy. Preventing future invasions requires the ability to predict which species will be successful invaders. Invading a new region often requires coping with novel environmental conditions, yet how invading populations adapt to environmental conditions encountered in their introduced range is not always clear. One process that may facilitate invasion in temperate environments is seasonal adaptive tracking, a rapid evolutionary process in which allele frequencies and phenotypes shift in response to seasonal environmental fluctuations, promoting the long-term maintenance of polymorphisms. Here, we test the hypothesis that adaptive tracking is a key contributor to the invasion success of the globally invasive fly Drosophila suzukii. We demonstrate that adaptive tracking results in predictable, rapid evolution of a key thermal tolerance trait (critical thermal minimum) essential for coping with climate variability. We also detect adaptive tracking in several genomic regions enriched for seasonally fluctuating alleles, and these alleles map to loci implicated in diverse traits, including thermal tolerance, pesticide resistance, and olfactory behavior. Finally, we find that loci undergoing adaptive tracking are significantly enriched for alleles associated with invasion in North American populations, suggesting that rapid evolution of seasonal traits may contribute to the success of this invasive species.

papers.title: Transcription factor handover reshapes hub dynamics to coordinate temporal progression of Notch response
papers.abstract: To decipher information in space and time, cells require mechanisms to sustain gene expression programmes once an initial signal decays. Localised condensation of transcription complexes into hubs is emerging as a key step in gene regulation and, by combining live imaging of transcription and of transcription complexes at target loci, we have investigated how these evolve to enable a prolonged transcription outcome in response to Notch signalling. Measuring the dynamics of hindsight (hnt) transcription reveals two phases. The first, a probabilistic response similar to E(spl)-C genes, is directly controlled by Notch and the second, a sustained response, is indirectly controlled through the BTB transcription factor Broad. The two phases correlate with a transition in transcription factor enrichment at hnt: complexes of Notch coactivator Mastermind and of Broad are successively enriched. Notably, the lifetime of the hubs formed by each are distinct and correlate with the change in transcription profiles. These reflect the binding dynamics of each complex, with Broad having significantly more stable association with chromatin, forming longer lasting hubs and yielding sustained transcription. Furthermore at intermediate stages we detect hubs containing both Broad and Mam implying an evolution in hub composition. Together our data support that the dynamic properties of transcription hubs are crucial for the probability and dynamics of transcription and point towards a ''hub handover'' in enabling temporal progression in gene expression responses.

papers.title: Metaplasia Orchestrates Tissue Recovery and Immune Remodeling Through CD73 in Chronic Pancreatitis
papers.abstract: Chronic inflammatory injury promotes epithelial metaplasia, and progression from metaplasia to dysplasia is a recognized initiating event in carcinogenesis, as metaplastic cells exhibit heightened susceptibility to genetic alterations. In the pancreas, persistent acinar-to-ductal metaplasia (ADM) can progress to pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN), yet the mechanisms that determine whether ADM resolves or persists with fibrosis and sustained inflammation remain poorly defined. Here, we identify CD73 as a central regulator of ADM fate, tissue repair, and immune microenvironment remodeling during chronic pancreatic injury. Analysis of previously published single-cell RNA sequencing dataset from chronic pancreatitis (CP) tissues identified enrichment of Nt5e, which encodes CD73, within Hnf1{beta} ADM populations. Hnf1bCreERT2 and CD73fl/fl;Hnf1bCreERT2 mice were treated with caerulein for 4 weeks to induce pancreatitis and ADM prior to tamoxifen-induced deletion of CD73 in HNF1B-expressing metaplastic epithelial cells. Histologic phenotyping and immune profiling were performed using immunohistochemistry and imaging mass cytometry. Metaplasia-specific CD73 deletion exacerbated pancreatic injury and fibrosis, impaired epithelial proliferation and recovery of the acinar compartment, and altered the abundance and spatial organization of inflammatory cells. Ex vivo ADM assays further demonstrated that CD73 loss increased ADM formation and the production of MCP-1 and TIMP-1. These findings identify CD73 as a context-dependent checkpoint linking epithelial plasticity and immune modulation during chronic pancreatic injury and tissue repair.

papers.title: HUH-tag conjugation enables accessible, site-specific functionalization of DNA origami with signaling-competent proteins
papers.abstract: DNA origami enables precise nanometer scale control over the number, spacing, and geometry of biomolecules, making it a powerful tool for dissecting spatially organized biological processes such as receptor signaling. However, functionalizing origami with proteins remains a bottleneck restricting the technology to specialized laboratories. Here we show that viral-derived HUH endonuclease tags, small (~10 kDa) domains that form a covalent phosphotyrosine bond with short unmodified ssDNA, provide a simple and cost-effective route to decorating DNA origami with functional proteins. Using interleukin-1{beta} (IL-1{beta}) as a model ligand, we generated recombinant IL-1{beta}-HUH, achieved efficient site-specific conjugation to unmodified ssDNA within minutes, and coupled the conjugates to a DNA origami pegboard with tunable stoichiometry. IL-1{beta}-functionalized origami triggered ligand-dependent signalling in living cells and allowed visualization of the recruitment of downstream signaling molecules, confirming that HUH-tag conjugation preserves functionality. Because this strategy requires only standard molecular biology equipment and unmodified DNA, it lowers a technical and financial barrier to DNA origami-based experimentation, opening the approach to a broader range of biological questions and laboratories outside the DNA nanotechnology field.

papers.title: A bivalent VP2 based vaccine approach reveals co expression driven interference between VP2 antigens impairing BTV neutralizing antibody induction
papers.abstract: Bluetongue virus (BTV) is an important arboviral pathogen of ruminants that causes a significant impact on the primary sector. More than 29 different BTV serotypes exist, hindering control and prevention of Bluetongue (BT) disease. Conventional vaccines possess safety and efficacy limitation and do not permit to confer multiserotype protection and differentiate between vaccinated and infected animals (DIVA strategy). Here, we developed recombinant Modified Vaccinia Ankara (rMVA) viral vectors individually expressing or co-expressing the neutralizing antibody (nAb) target proteins VP2 of BTV serotypes 4 and 8. We evaluated their immunogenicity and protective efficacy in IFNAR(-/-) mice and sheep. Immunization of IFNAR(-/-) mice with the rMVA co-expressing of BTV-4 VP2 and BTV-8 VP2 led to abolished nAb induction while eliciting non neutralizing antibodies against both VP2 proteins, suggesting a previously unrecognized interference between VP2 antigens. Combined immunization of IFNAR(-/-) mice with rMVAs expressing either BTV-4 VP2 or BTV-8 VP2 elicited a strong neutralizing immune response and complete protection against lethal challenge with BTV-4 or BTV-8. In sheep, combinatorial prime-boost immunization with these monovalent rMVAs induced nAbs against both homologous BTV serotypes. Immunized sheep were fully protected against BTV-4, as no fever or viral replication were detected after challenge. Similarly, immunized sheep were also protected against BTV-8 although detectable but mild RNAemia and slight increase in rectal temperatures were observed after challenge. Overall, we identified a relevant constraint for multivalent VP2 based vaccine design and present a DIVA vaccination strategy that offers bivalent protection against BTV in a natural host of the disease.

papers.title: Outbreaks of Newcastle Disease Virus Genotype VII.1.1 in Vaccinated Commercial Poultry, Germany, 2026
papers.abstract: During February-May 2026, Newcastle disease virus subgenotype VII.1.1, related to viruses circulating in Eastern Europe, caused Germany's first major outbreaks in decades, despite mandatory poultry vaccination programs. Clinical signs ranged from inapparent to severe, with low recorded mortality. These findings highlight the need for enhanced surveillance beyond clinical disease detection.

papers.title: MLL4 regulates palatal salivary gland development
papers.abstract: Palatal glands are minor mucous salivary glands that contribute to oral lubrication and mucosal defense through the secretion of mucus and protective factors such as secretory immunoglobulin A. They are also the most common site of benign and malignant minor salivary gland tumors. Despite their physiological and clinical importance, the molecular mechanisms underlying palatal gland development remain poorly understood. Given the essential role of the epigenetic regulator MLL4 (KMT2D) in craniofacial development, we investigated its role in palatal gland development using a conditional knockout (cKO) mouse model with tissue-specific deletion of Mll4 in the palatal mesenchyme (Mll4fl/fl;Osr2-Cre). Mll4-cKO mice exhibited palatal gland hypoplasia from birth through adulthood, accompanied by ectopic cartilage formation in the soft palate. RNA-seq analysis revealed downregulation of genes and biological processes associated with salivary gland development, branching morphogenesis, and FGF and WNT signaling, together with upregulation of biological processes related to chondrocyte proliferation, consistent with the glandular hypoplasia and ectopic cartilage phenotypes. In situ hybridization and immunofluorescence analyses confirmed reduced mesenchymal Fgf10 expression, decreased epithelial SOX9 and Edar expression, and localized accumulation of SOX9-positive cells within the ectopic cartilage. Ki67 immunostaining demonstrated reduced epithelial cell proliferation without altered apoptosis in Mll4-cKO palatal glands. Collectively, these findings identify MLL4 as an essential epigenetic regulator of palatal gland morphogenesis that coordinates mesenchymal-epithelial signaling while maintaining normal developmental programs within the soft palate.

papers.title: Ribosome remodeling under glucotoxic conditions impairs beta-cell function
papers.abstract: Diabetes develops when pancreatic beta-cells fail to secrete sufficient insulin to meet metabolic demand. Chronic hyperglycemia accelerates beta-cell failure and dysregulates mRNA translation before the onset of endoplasmic reticulum stress, but the underlying mechanisms remain unknown. Here, quantitative mass spectrometry of translating ribosomes isolated from MIN6 cells under control and glucotoxic conditions revealed that sustained high glucose remodels ribosome composition by selectively decreasing Ribosomal Protein Lateral Stalk Subunit P1 (RPLP1) on actively translating ribosomes. Knockdown of RPLP1 in MIN6 cells and in primary islets reduced translation of insulin and impaired glucose-stimulated insulin secretion. Depletion of RPLP1 in vivo led to glucose intolerance. Together, our findings indicate that glucotoxicity remodels beta-cell ribosomes, leading to selective mRNA translation impairment and decreased insulin secretion. This previously unrecognized mechanism linking metabolic overload to beta-cell dysfunction suggests that preserving RPLP1 association with ribosomes could represent a therapeutic strategy for maintaining beta-cell function in diabetes.

papers.title: Candidatus Pannonibacter alzirae sp. nov. isolated from a septic immunocompromised patient in Brazil
papers.abstract: Pannonibacter species. are non-fermentative Gram-stain-negative bacteria, with rare reports of human infections primarily affecting immunocompromised patients. Here, we report the genomic and phenotypic characterization of a novel Pannonibacter species, isolated from a bacteremia episode in a pediatric patient with acute lymphoblastic leukemia in Brazil. Initial characterization of the isolate (here named CBAS 1226) by MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry and 16S ribosomal RNA gene sequencing identified it as Pannonibacter sp., most closely related to P. phragmitetus. However, comparison of its MALDI-TOF spectrum with a commercial reference library revealed compatibility with only two of the five main spectra profiles for P. phragmitetus. This discrepancy motivated comprehensive genomic, biochemical, morphological, and antimicrobial resistance profiling of CBAS 1226. Genomic analysis revealed that Pannonibacter sp. CBAS 1226 is phylogenetically distinct from P. phragmitetus and other known species, with ANI and dDDH values below species delineation thresholds, supporting its proposal as Candidatus Pannonibacter alzirae. It forms small, non-hemolytic, grayish-white colonies on blood agar, similar to its closest relatives P. phragmitetus and P. indicus. Phenotypically, it is distinguished by positive - and {beta}-glucosidase activity, along with the utilization of citrate, L-proline, and 2-ketoglutarate. It is negative for alkaline phosphatase and unable to utilize D-fructose, D-melibiose, esculin, or L-arginine. The isolate exhibited higher MICs for {beta}-lactams, whereas carbapenems and fluoroquinolones showed low MICs. The isolate is capable of forming biofilms and tolerates alkaline conditions, a wide range of temperatures, and different oxygen concentrations. Altogether, this report emphasizes the relevance of additional proteomics- and genomics-based approaches to clarify unusual bacterial infections and describes a new Pannonibacter species with distinct features and the potential to cause opportunistic infections.

papers.title: Cryo-EM Structure of Mycobacteriophage D29 Reveals a Specialized Portal-Capsid Junction and a Unique 13-Subunit Baseplate Collar
papers.abstract: Mycobacteriophages are promising agents against drug-resistant mycobacterial infections, yet their structural organization and host-recognition mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we determined cryo-EM structures of the capsid, connector, tail tube, and baseplate of the lytic, broad-host-range mycobacteriophage D29, revealing a near-complete virion architecture. At the capsid-portal interface, five copies of the previously uncharacterized protein gp19.1 bridge adjacent capsid subunits around the dodecameric portal, potentially reinforcing the symmetry-mismatched vertex. At the baseplate, 13 copies of gp6 assemble into a collar surrounding the sixfold-symmetric gp23-gp27 core. Remarkably, this 6:13 symmetry mismatch is accommodated through six distinct gp6- gp27 interfaces involving 12 gp6 subunits, leaving one subunit largely disengaged from the core. This asymmetric organization produces a tilted, outward-flaring collar that presents an extensive surface with the potential to engage the host cell. Whole-cell binding and plaque-competition assays further implicate the gp6 collar and the flexible trimeric central fiber gp31 in host recognition. Together, these findings reveal distinct structural adaptations at symmetry-mismatched interfaces and provide a structural framework for understanding mycobacteriophage assembly and host engagement.

papers.title: Antibody design across observed and forecasted antigenic evolution
papers.abstract: The therapeutic efficacy of antibodies is often limited by the evolution of their targets. Designing or eliciting antibodies that withstand such evolution is challenging as their binding interfaces must accommodate antigenic variation. Here, we introduce Germinal Multi, a computational framework for de novo antibody design and rescue that jointly optimizes a single paratope against multiple antigenic variants. We applied Germinal Multi to cancer and viral antigens, targeting both observed antigenic variation and prospective antibody escape. Multi-target optimization yielded antibodies that bound resistance-associated EGFR variants or that neutralized antigenically distinct historical SARS-CoV-2 variants, with recognition extending to variants withheld from the design process. Beyond acting on observed evolution, we redesigned the broadly neutralizing antibody BD55-1205 to restore neutralization of a prospective escape variant engineered with guidance from an evolutionary forecasting model, while preserving activity against the parental variant. Successful candidates were identified after screening tens of designs per campaign. Together, these results establish multi-target computational design as a strategy for generating antibody breadth across observed antigenic variation and demonstrate the potential of evolutionary forecasting to guide antibody redesign against prospective escape.
